title: The House of Marrow Creek
premise: Rafael Vasquez, a skeptical property surveyor sent to appraise the derelict Hollis house in Marrow Creek, discovers the village's church bell—melted down in 1911—ringing from the house's attic every night at 3:11 a.m. As the frost on the windows begins forming patterns that map the house room by room, Rafael uncovers a century-old pact: in 1911 the villagers melted the bell to hide evidence of a drowning they committed, and the house has been 'appraising' souls ever since, taking one each winter. To survive until sunrise and end the cycle, Rafael must publicly confess what the village invited in—not with their own name, but with the truth of the original crime—and accept that justice outside the law demands a price: they can leave alive only if they carry the house's ledger out with them, becoming its next keeper.
about_author: Jude Crane is the pen name of a former rural assessor who spent a decade appraising abandoned properties across New England before turning to horror. They write in unheated farmhouses, insisting the drafts improve the prose.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Rafael Vasquez arrives in Marrow Creek to appraise the long-vacant Hollis house, armed with instruments and disbelief. The village is oddly hostile; no one will meet their eyes. In the house, Rafael notes impossible measurements—a hallway longer inside than out—and dismisses it as settling foundations. POV: Rafael. Emotional beat: professional detachment masking a loneliness that makes them easy prey for a place that notices.

chapters.title: Frostwork
chapters.summary: Overnight frost forms on the interior windows in precise patterns: floor plans, dates, names. Rafael photographs everything and tells themselves it's condensation. At the general store, an old woman, Edith Marsh, warns them not to stay past dark and calls the house 'the auditor.' POV: Rafael. Emotional beat: creeping unease sharpened by the villagers' complicit silence—the first hint this is a town keeping a secret, not just a haunted house.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't
chapters.summary: At 3:11 a.m., a bell tolls from the attic. Rafael climbs up and finds a rope hanging from nothing, a scorch mark shaped like a bell, and parish records confirming St. Alban's bell was melted down in 1911. The frost now spells a name: THOMAS HOLLIS. POV: Rafael. Emotional beat: skepticism cracking into dread; the house isn't haunting—it's itemizing.

chapters.title: Ledger of Small Sins
chapters.summary: Rafael finds a ledger in the cellar listing every villager since 1911, each entry ending in a winter date. Edith finally talks: in 1911 the village drowned a traveling bell-founder, Thomas Hollis, and melted his bell to destroy the evidence. The house took the bell's place. Every winter it collects. POV: alternating Rafael and Edith. Emotional beat: guilt inherited like property; loyalty to kin versus truth.

chapters.title: What Was Invited
chapters.summary: Rafael learns the appraisal request was signed by someone dead forty years—the house invited them. Trapped by a snowstorm, they try to leave; the road loops back to the front gate. The frost patterns now include Rafael's own name, dated tomorrow. POV: Rafael. Emotional beat: terror curdling into fury—they were summoned as this year's payment.

chapters.title: The Village That Looks Away
chapters.summary: Rafael confronts the villagers, who admit the arrangement: look away, live long. Edith's brother was taken in 1987 because she once tried to speak. The constable offers Rafael a deal—sign off on the appraisal, forget everything, drive out at dawn. POV: Rafael with Edith present. Emotional beat: the seduction of complicity; survival offered at the price of becoming one more pair of looking-away eyes.

chapters.title: Room by Room
chapters.summary: The house begins rearranging itself along the frost-map, sealing exits and herding Rafael through rooms that replay 1911: the drowned man's coat still dripping, the forge still hot. Rafael realizes the house doesn't want a death—it wants a verdict. POV: Rafael. Emotional beat: claustrophobic escalation; the past is not remembered here, it is rehearsed nightly.

The final night. The bell rings continuously. Villagers gather outside the fence, some begging Rafael to sign, Edith urging them to speak. The frost completes a pattern across every window: a courtroom. Rafael understands the terms—confess the crime aloud, name the guilty, and the house will judge whether truth outweighs a hundred years of silence. POV: Rafael. Emotional beat: the choice crystallizes; loyalty to the living village against truth owed to the dead.

chapters.title: The Verdict of Frost
chapters.summary: At sunrise's edge, Rafael stands in the attic and speaks Thomas Hollis's name and the village's crime into the ringing dark. The bell falls silent mid-toll. The frost writes one last line—PAID IN FULL?—and the house waits. Rafael refuses to name a single scapegoat and instead names everyone who looked away, including themselves for nearly signing. The windows shatter outward. POV: Rafael. Emotional beat: climax—justice demanded without mercy, including self-indictment.

chapters.title: The New Keeper
chapters.summary: Rafael walks out at dawn into a village that won't meet their eyes, carrying the ledger under their arm—the price of exit. The house stands empty, appraised at nothing, though the frost never quite leaves its windows. In the epilogue beat, Rafael mails a copy of the ledger to every household in Marrow Creek and keeps the original, learning its pages have begun listing new names. POV: Rafael. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution—survived, but bound; truth delivered, but now Rafael is the one who keeps the accounts.
